title: Learning Fast Approximations of Sparse Coding

citations.claim: Gregor and LeCun introduced LISTA (Learned ISTA), the foundational algorithm unrolling method that unfolds a fixed number of ISTA iterations into a feed-forward neural network with learned parameters, achieving roughly 20 times faster convergence than FISTA for approximate sparse coding.

LISTA replaces the matrices W_e and S in ISTA, which are normally computed from the dictionary and sparsity parameters, with learned matrices optimized end-to-end via backpropagation to minimize the squared error between predicted and optimal sparse codes.

Gregor and LeCun demonstrated that a trained K-layer LISTA network can be viewed as a time-unfolded recurrent neural network with shared weights across layers, to which backpropagation through time is applied for training.

LISTA with a single iteration achieved prediction error of 1.50 for 100-unit codes, compared to 21.0 for FISTA with one iteration, demonstrating that learning the iteration parameters dramatically improves per-iteration efficiency.
Gregor and LeCun showed that it takes 18 iterations of FISTA to reach the same error as 1 iteration of LISTA for 100-dimensional codes, and 35 iterations for 400-dimensional codes.

The LISTA architecture implements approximate explaining away between code components through the learned mutual inhibition matrix S, enabling competition between basis functions that simple feed-forward encoders cannot achieve.

Gregor and LeCun also proposed Learned Coordinate Descent (LCoD), which learns the matrices in a truncated coordinate descent algorithm, achieving approximately 20 times speedup over standard CoD with per-iteration cost of O(m) instead of O(m^2).
The LISTA encoder is differentiable with respect to both its parameters and its input, enabling it to be incorporated into larger globally-trained recognition systems via backpropagation.

Gregor and LeCun established the paradigm of algorithm unrolling, where an iterative optimization algorithm is truncated to a fixed depth and its parameters are learned end-to-end, trading generality for speed on a specific data distribution.

The LISTA framework trains a nonlinear feed-forward predictor with a specific architecture and fixed depth to produce the best possible approximation of the sparse code for inputs drawn from the training distribution.

do_not_claim: LISTA converges to the true optimal code when run for more steps than trained
LISTA was applied to baseline correction, chromatography, or signal denoising
LISTA learns only scalar parameters per layer
